When Mr. Hiram B. Otis, the American Minister, bought Canterville Chase, everyone told him he was making a foolish decision: the place was unquestionably haunted. Lord Canterville himself, a man with an exceptionally exacting sense of honour, had felt obliged to explain this when he and Mr. Otis discussed the sale.

‘We haven’t wanted to live there ourselves,’ Lord Canterville said, ‘since my great-aunt, the Dowager Duchess of Bolton, suffered a fit of terror from which she never fully recovered. Two skeletal hands were placed on her shoulders while she was dressing for dinner. I should also tell you, Mr. Otis, that several living members of my family have seen the ghost, as has the parish rector, the Reverend Augustus Dampier, a Fellow of King’s College, Cambridge. After the Duchess’s unfortunate experience, none of our younger servants would stay, and Lady Canterville often barely slept because of the mysterious noises coming from the corridor and the library.’

‘My Lord,’ the Minister replied, ‘I’m happy to buy the furniture and the ghost at their estimated value. I come from a modern country, where we have everything money can buy. With all our energetic young men tearing around the Old World and carrying off your finest actresses and opera singers, I figure that if Europe had a ghost, we’d soon have it back home, either in one of our public museums or touring as an attraction.’

‘I’m afraid the ghost does exist,’ said Lord Canterville, smiling, ‘though it may have turned down your enterprising theatrical promoters. It has been well known for three centuries—since 1584, to be precise—and always appears before someone in our family dies.’

‘Well, so does the family doctor, Lord Canterville, when you think about it. But there are no such things as ghosts, sir, and I don’t suppose the laws of nature will be suspended for the benefit of the British aristocracy.’

‘Americans certainly are very natural,’ replied Lord Canterville, who had not quite understood Mr. Otis’s last comment. ‘And if you’re willing to have a ghost in the house, that’s perfectly all right. Just remember that I warned you.’

A few weeks later the purchase was finalised, and at the end of the social season the Minister and his family travelled down to Canterville Chase. Mrs. Otis had once been the celebrated New York beauty Miss Lucretia R. Tappan of West 53rd Street. Now middle-aged, she remained a very handsome woman, with lovely eyes and a magnificent profile.

When I returned, I found this letter from my father:

‘My dear Victor,

‘You have probably been waiting impatiently for a letter settling the date of your return home. At first I was tempted to write just a few lines telling you when to come. But that would be a cruel kindness, and I cannot bring myself to do it. Imagine your shock, my son, if you arrived expecting a joyful welcome and found tears and misery instead. Yet how can I tell you what has happened, Victor? Your absence cannot have made you indifferent to our happiness and grief. How am I to cause such pain to the son who has been away from me so long? I want to prepare you for this terrible news, though I know that is impossible. Even now your eyes are racing down the page in search of the words that will tell you the worst.

‘William is dead! That dear child whose smile delighted and warmed my heart, so gentle and yet so full of joy! Victor, he has been murdered!

‘I will not try to comfort you. I will simply tell you the circumstances.

‘Last Thursday, May 7th, my niece, your two brothers, and I went walking in Plainpalais. The evening was warm and peaceful, and we walked farther than usual. Dusk had already fallen when we thought of turning back. Then we realised that William and Ernest, who had gone ahead, were nowhere to be seen. We sat down to wait for them. Before long Ernest returned and asked whether we had seen his brother. They had been playing together, he said, when William ran off to hide. Ernest had searched without success and then waited a long time, but William had never reappeared.

‘This worried us, and we kept searching until nightfall. Then Elizabeth suggested that he might have gone home. He was not there. We went back with torches, for I could not rest while imagining my sweet boy lost outside, exposed to the night’s damp and dew. Elizabeth, too, was terribly distressed. At about five in the morning I found my beautiful boy, whom I had seen so healthy and lively the evening before, lying discoloured and motionless on the grass. The mark of the murderer’s finger was on his neck.

‘He was carried home, and the anguish in my face told Elizabeth what had happened. She insisted on seeing his body. At first I tried to stop her, but she would not give way. Entering the room where he lay, she quickly examined the victim’s neck, clasped her hands, and cried, “Oh God!’

‘But don’t imagine I didn’t consider it a bad thing in itself.’

‘You can be certain they were all perfectly comfortable.’

‘That might not make me like them any better. That many women and children have no right to be comfortable on a ship.’

‘My dear Frederick, you’re talking nonsense. What would happen to us poor sailors’ wives if everyone thought as you do? We often need passage from one port to another to join our husbands.’

‘My opinions, as you see, didn’t stop me taking Mrs Harville and her entire family to Plymouth.’

‘But I dislike hearing you speak like some grand gentleman, as though women were all delicate ladies instead of sensible people. None of us expects smooth sailing all our lives.’

‘Ah, my dear,’ said the Admiral, ‘he’ll change his tune once he has a wife. When he’s married, if we’re fortunate enough to live to see another war, we’ll watch him do just what you and I, and plenty of others, have done. He’ll be grateful to anyone willing to bring his wife to him.’

‘Yes, he certainly will.’

‘Then I give up,’ Captain Wentworth exclaimed. ‘Once married people start in on me with “Oh, you’ll think quite differently when you’re married,” all I can say is “No, I won’t.” Then they say “Yes, you will,” and that settles the matter.’

He stood up and walked away.

‘You must have travelled a great deal, ma’am!’ Mrs Musgrove said to Mrs Croft.

‘A fair amount in fifteen years of marriage, ma’am, though many women have travelled more. I’ve crossed the Atlantic four times, and been to the East Indies and back once—just the once. And we’ve been to various places closer to home: Cork, Lisbon, Gibraltar. But I’ve never been beyond the Straits or visited the West Indies. We don’t count Bermuda or the Bahamas as the West Indies, you know.’

Mrs Musgrove could offer no disagreement. She could not remember ever having called them anything at all in her entire life.

‘And I assure you, ma’am,’ Mrs Croft continued, ‘nothing could be more comfortable than the accommodation on a warship. I mean the larger classes, of course. On a frigate there’s naturally less room, though any reasonable woman can be perfectly happy aboard one. I can honestly say that the happiest years of my life have been spent at sea. As long as we were together, you see, there was nothing to fear.’
